title: Rotate a VCF Automation cloud account credential without stranding in-flight requests
prompt:
The payments platform's VCF Automation cloud account `ca-9f41d7b0-5c2e-4a18-bd93-0e7c6a1f4a22` points at a production vCenter, and the service account it authenticates with is due for its quarterly secret rotation. Last quarter someone rotated it from the UI in the middle of a provisioning wave and half a dozen deployments died part-way through: they had been admitted under the old password, they kept presenting it to vCenter, and by the time they got to their next provider call the platform had already replaced it. There was nothing clean to roll back to. We want the rotation driven from PowerShell this time, and we want it to refuse to strand anything.

The repository has the skeleton of a module for this, `VcfAutomation.CredentialRotation`, with both of its public functions throwing `NotImplementedException`. Implement them while preserving their existing public parameter lists and documented output shapes.

VCF Automation has no published API specification, so `docs/contract.json` is a hand-transcribed contract derived from the Broadcom xAPIs reference pages for the VM Apps Org Provisioning Service; `docs/official_sources.json` records which page each part came from. Treat the contract as authoritative and do not widen it — it names five operations and that is the whole surface the client may touch. VCF PowerCLI (`VMware.Sdk.Vcf.*`) is already installed and is declared in the module manifest; don't vendor a copy of it into the repo.

What the rotation has to do:

- Drain before it rotates. List the request trackers, and for anything still `INPROGRESS`, follow it until it reaches `FINISHED` or `FAILED`. Only once nothing is in flight may the update go out.
- Read the account before it writes it. `name`, `cloudAccountProperties` and `regions` are all required on the update, so carry the first two forward unchanged and build `regions` from the account's current `enabledRegions`. Changing a password must not quietly drop the endpoint's hostname or its enabled regions.
- Treat `202 Accepted` as "queued", not "done". Both the update and the health check hand back a request tracker; follow each to a terminal status.
- Health-check the endpoint afterwards, once the update has actually finished, so we know the new secret works.
- Send only the fields we mean to set. This is a PATCH: a field that is present but empty is a request to clear it, so an optional field we aren't setting has to be absent from the JSON entirely — not `null`, not `""`, not `[]`. A caller who explicitly passes an empty value does mean to clear it, and that must still go on the wire.
- Keep the new secret in the `privateKey` field of the update body and nowhere else. No URLs, no query strings, no headers.

`tests/Invoke-Verification.ps1` runs the module against a loopback mock of the API and checks the exact shape of every request it made. Run it with `pwsh -File tests/Invoke-Verification.ps1`.
